eye.because: Order: the four frames form one cumulative sequence, and the same sequence shows in all four views. B is the clearest case. In Z it is a plain symmetrical dwelling: door in the middle, a window each side, window boxes, no sign, no fascia. I read that as the original arrangement. In Y a fascia, blank board panels, a pair of doors and a dark hanging box have replaced the ground-floor windows, so B has become a shop or store. In W and X a glazed veranda with a balcony above has been added on the left. A has a plate-glass shopfront with a fascia in Z, Y and W. In X that shopfront has gone and the two domestic ground-floor windows are back, so a shop was closed and its front removed. The distant house D gives the same split: its three gable windows are boarded in Y and Z and glazed again in W and X. Direction: I take the order as earliest Z to latest X, because additions (shop conversion, veranda) accumulate and persist, and the only loss is one shopfront. The reverse would need the veranda, the shop and the window trim all removed again, which is less natural for a building history. Years: these are guesses (confidence 1 on the years themselves). I judged the plate-glass shop front to be late 19th century, and the glazed veranda to be roughly 1900 to 1930. I put the closure of A's shop and the return of its domestic windows after the mid-century. The spacing is judged from how many changes each step adds.

street.because: C's windows are the clearest clue. In W both the front windows and the gable-end window are plain, with no surround. In Z and X the gable window has a casing with a sill, but the front windows are still plain. In Y the front windows also have casings and sills. The trim builds up in that order, plain then gable-end trim then all trim. I read the plain, trimless state as the oldest. D's loft window is boarded (W, Z) or glazed with a casing (X, Y). The small house E at the top of the lane is the other way round: its windows are lit and glazed in W and Z, and boarded or shuttered in X and Y. So the boarding moves from D to E between the second and third frames. Matched to the eye view, W is the state with B still a house, and Y is the state with A's shopfront gone. The order is the same as in the other views. Years are guesses, the same four dates as in the other views.

12m.because: C's gable-end window is plain with no casing in X only. In W, Z and Y it has a casing and a sill. C's lower front window has the fuller casing and glazing bars only in Y, so Y is the most elaborated, latest state. D's gable windows are boarded in X and W (all three have X-bracing) and glazed in Z and Y. E at the top of the lane is glazed in X and W and boarded in Z and Y. The cumulative order is therefore X, W, Z, Y. Each of these features matches the same feature in the street, eye and city views. Years are guesses, the same four dates as in the other views.

city.because: From above, the changes are small and local; the rest of the town is identical in all four, so I see no new building or demolition. C's gable window is plain in X and casing-trimmed in W, Y and Z, so X is the earliest. B has no veranda in X and W. In X its ground floor looks like windows, and in W it has the blank-panel shop front. B has the veranda from the side in Y and Z. A's ground floor has the large shopfront window in X, W and Y. It is replaced by ordinary domestic windows only in Z. The houses D and E at the head of the lane match the other views: D is glazed and E is boarded from Y on. These features give the cumulative order X, W, Y, Z. The years are the same guesses as in the other views.
